title: TLS zero-byte read + MTU probing scratchpad
content:
Goal:
Quick brain-dump of everything tried and open hypotheses for the TLS 0-byte-read symptom observed on private deployments that use VPC peering / TGW egress to internet. Intended as a personal checklist and handoff note.

Summary of symptom:
- App containers intermittently see TLS handshakes fail with "0 bytes read" (client logs) when connecting to external vendors (SaaS APIs) over TCP/443.
- Failures are transient (typically 10s-120s window) and recover without infra changes.
- Affects clients behind peered VPCs (VPC-A -> Transit-GW -> egress VPC/ENI).
- No obvious application-layer rejection (server certs look fine when successful).

Context / environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC) mimicking prod routing through TGW/IGW NAT on egress account.
- Primary instances: c6i.large-like (Linux kernel 5.10+), iptables NAT, conntrack enabled.
- BGP peering between data center and VPC? No. This is AWS-only multi-account TGW.

Timeline (recent run):
- 2025-11-04 09:13 UTC: spike of 503s in app logs with "tls: TLS handshake error: remote error: unexpected message" and some "read: connection reset by peer".
- 2025-11-04 09:14 UTC: manual curl -> works. But curl from same pod intermittently returns "56 recv failure: Connection reset by peer".

Commands / probes I ran (raw):
- curl --verbose --connect-timeout 5 https://api.vendor.example/health
  * Reused, sometimes succeeds.
  * On failure: "* Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed" or curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer

- openssl s_client -connect api.vendor.example:443 -servername api.vendor.example -tls1_2
  CONNECTED(00000003)
  140736...:error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number:
  --- sometimes the server sends a short TCP RST mid-handshake.

- ss -tanp | grep 443
  ESTAB  0      0   10.0.2.15:51982   52.23.44.10:443   
  TIME_WAIT 0      0   10.0.2.15:52000   52.23.44.10:443

- sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 'tcp port 443' -w /tmp/trace.pcap (during failure window)
  Observed pattern: client SYN -> server SYN/ACK -> client ACK, then ~200ms later server sends small segment with FIN or RST without completing TLS handshake. In some traces we see repeated small segments (size 0) flagged as "TCP zero window" then RST.

Small tcpdump excerpt (annotated):
  09:13:02.123456 IP 10.0.2.15.51982 > 52.23.44.10.443: Flags [S], seq 12345
  09:13:02.124121 IP 52.23.44.10.443 > 10.0.2.15.51982: Flags [S.], seq 99999, ack 12346
  09:13:02.124200 IP 10.0.2.15.51982 > 52.23.44.10.443: Flags [.], ack 100000
  09:13:02.324900 IP 52.23.44.10.443 > 10.0.2.15.51982: Flags [.], seq 100000, ack 12346, win 0  <-- server advertised zero window
  09:13:02.325100 IP 52.23.44.10.443 > 10.0.2.15.51982: Flags [R], seq 100001  <-- RST shortly after

Hypothesis 1: PMTU / fragmentation causing middlebox to drop larger TLS records or trigger zero-window behavior
- Rationale: failures correlate with slightly larger TLS ClientHello sizes (SNI + ALPN + cert compression etc). If path MTU smaller than expected and there's filtering of fragmented IP fragments (or ICMP unreachable filtered), we can get stalls or abrupt resets.
- What I tried: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 (enabled) on a test node -> reduced incidence in test session but not fully mitigated.
- Tools: sudo ping -M do -s 1472 api.vendor.example (fragmentation test) -> sometimes returns "Frag needed and DF set (ICMP)" from intermediate IP, but many peered routes obfuscate ICMP.
- Next: schedule iperf3 with -M to vary MSS and observe.

Hypothesis 2: ECMP / asymmetric routing + conntrack NAT timeouts lead to server seeing different source path and resetting
- Rationale: TGW can choose different attachments on retransmits; if NAT mapping lost or re-created on second path, server may reject.
- What I tried: Inspect conntrack counters during reproductions: sudo conntrack -L | grep 52.23.44.10
  Found entries showing RELATED,UNTRACKED in certain bursts. conntrack table size near limit (nf_conntrack_count ~ 640k / table 655360).
- Mitigation tried: increase conntrack max, but symptom persisted. Possibly a race rather than table capacity.

Hypothesis 3: TCP offloads / TSO/GRO interfering with capture/seq numbers across virtualization and TGW
- Rationale: Some guesstimates point to zero-window in tcpdump but kernel still has bytes; GRO/TSO can make captures misleading.
- What I tried: ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off on a test node -> tcpdump trace looked more faithful, but issue still occurred rarely. Not conclusive.

Hypothesis 4: Vendor-side abuse protection or middlebox actively aborting perceived suspicious flows mid-handshake (e.g., IDS sees fragment, drops)
- Rationale: Vendor previously rolled out WAF rules in the same timeframe; correlation in PagerDuty notes.
- What I tried: contacted vendor security, they reported no changes.

Other interesting artifacts:
- curl --tcp-fastopen sometimes reduces latency but not failure rate.
- strace -f -e trace=network on client process shows connect() succeeds then read() returns 0 (EOF) during handshake.
- iptables NAT logs: some SNAT rules hit counters in bursts; used iptables -S -t nat and -L -v -n to review.

Quick checklist to reproduce reliably:
1) Start a pod with curl in peered-private-subnet (same AZ as TGW attachment)
2) Run continuous curl loop with -v and log timestamps: while true; do date -u +%s%3N; curl -v --max-time 6 https://api.vendor.example/health || echo "FAIL $(date -u)"; sleep 0.2; done
3) Capture tcpdump on the pod's ENI and on the egress ENI/NAT gateway simultaneously (requires SRE permission)
4) Correlate with TGW flow logs (if enabled) and VPC flow logs.

Ideas for next experiments (ordered):
- Try forcing MSS clamp at instance level: iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --set-mss 1200. See if client hello sizes are reduced and failures drop.
- Spin up a minimal public EC2 in same region and replicate egress without TGW (direct IGW) to compare.
- Run tcpdump on host (before NAT) and on NAT gateway to check whether server sees fragments or different syn/ack pattern.
- Enable tcpdump with -s 0 to capture full payload for single failing handshake (legal/PII ok since this is test vendor health endpoint).
- Mock vendor endpoint in our lab to reproduce with controlled MTU/amplification (drop ICMP unreachable to emulate path filtering).
- Schedule a brief window to toggle net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing back to 0 to compare.
- Add temporary MTU clamping on TGW attachment (if possible) or adjust route tables to force path with high MTU.

Notes to handoff (if I get paged):
- Primary suspects: path MTU + middlebox filtering OR transient conntrack/NAT inconsistency during ECMP path changes.
- If asked to mitigate quickly: apply TCPMSS clamp on outbound nodes to 1200 as temporary mitigation (low risk).
- If asked for durable fix: need SRE to correlate TGW flow logs + ENI captures + NAT gateway logs. Possibly request vendor to return server-side logs at timestamps.

Open questions:
- Are there CloudFront / WAF / vendor-side load balancers applying blackbox rewriting of TLS records?
- Is there a correlation with AZ failovers or route table changes around the timestamps?
- Do we see similar patterns for other vendors or only this SaaS?

Raw scratch commands to rerun quickly:
- sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1
- sudo ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off
- sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 'tcp port 443' -w /tmp/failtrace.pcap &
- sudo iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --set-mss 1200
- iperf3 -c <test-server> -M 1200 -p 5201 -t 60

If I don't get back to this: assign INF-1723 to SRE with request for synchronized captures (pod ENI + natgw + vendor timestamp matching).

Short-term TODOs (me):
- [ ] Run controlled iperf3/MSS matrix and capture on both ends (this week).
- [ ] Try TCPMSS clamp on one node to see if errors fall (low risk) (today).
- [ ] Ask SRE to enable TGW flow logs for the window and share (create ticket).
- [ ] Reach out to vendor again with exact UTC timestamps and sample pcap (if allowed) to get server-side logs.

End of scratchpad.

Notes: this is intentionally messy — quick copy to Confluence later if we find persistent repro.
